summary: Believable twin-tether pedestal charger with good UI and label decals; the cables, plugs and plinth hold it back.
critique: Proportions are right for a pedestal charger: about 1.4-1.5 m tall, a slim rectangular body, a green cap, a 22 kW AC badge, a screen with legible UI, a tap-card pad, a QR code, an LED status bar, a hazard label, a vent grille and a rear info plate. It reads instantly as the real thing. Problems: (1) The two connectors are chunky square-section blocks with flat faces and hard edges. A Type 2 handle is a rounded, ergonomic pistol grip with a round 7-pin face and a hinged cap, and here they read as grey boxes. The holsters are plain cuboids too. (2) The cable path is unconvincing. The cable leaves the plug, rises above the holster, then drops in a long, perfectly smooth, constant-radius loop and re-enters the body through a small gland low on the side. Real tethered cables are thicker (about 25-30 mm), coil or hang over a hook, and have some slack and contact with the plinth or ground. These loops are uniform, too thin in the side view (nearly a ribbon) and cast an odd floating shadow. (3) The body is a perfect box: no draft on the panels, no rubber gasket line between the cap and the body, and the door seam is only drawn on, with no recess. (4) The concrete plinth is a clean slab: no chamfer, no weathering, no anchor bolts beyond a thin steel base frame, no kerb or bollard protection. (5) The cap is a flat-topped green box with a slight bevel. Real units have a moulded overhang with a drip edge. (6) The surfaces are very clean, with only light grime at the base.
suggestions: Rebuild each connector as a lathe-plus-loft handle: a 40 mm round nose with a 7-hole face decal, a 35 mm grip tapering to a cable strain-relief boot, and a hinged dust cap (about 300 tris each). Make the holster an angled cup that matches the nose (about 120 tris).

Make the cable 26 mm diameter with 8 sides (12 at hero LOD). Route it along a catenary: from the plug boot down to touch the plinth or ground, lying on it for 0.2-0.4 m, then up into a rubber gland about 0.5 m above the base. Add a slight random sag per instance. Do not use perfect circular loops.
Chamfer the body edges by 8-10 mm. Inset the access door 3 mm with a real seam and a cylinder lock. Add a 15 mm darker rubber gasket band under the cap. Give the cap a 20 mm overhang and drip edge.

Plinth: 15 mm edge chamfer, 4 visible M16 anchor nuts, dirt and water staining darker at the base (albedo about 0.35 to 0.25). Optionally add a yellow-topped steel protection bollard or a wheel stop as a variant.

Wear pass in the existing atlas: finger grime around the screen and RFID pad, UV-faded green on the cap top, a sticker residue patch, and roughness rising from 0.35 to 0.6 near the base. Cost: one 1K mask, no extra draws.
renderer_notes: With no SSR or GI, the dark cable and the screen bezel look flatter than they would in an engine with reflections. The sky and lawn are not the asset's fault.

summary: Correct idea (a stack of four plus one leaning) but the tyres are low-poly, have no sidewall moulding, and the tread is painted on.
critique: Car tyres at the right scale (about 600-650 mm OD, 205-225 section) with a slightly offset stack and one tyre leaning against it, which is a nice narrative touch. However: (1) The silhouette is faceted. The leaning tyre's outer rim and bead show clear polygon steps in the close-up, and tyres are a pure silhouette object, so this is the first thing that reads as CG. (2) The tread is a normal or albedo pattern on a smooth cylinder. There are no real grooves breaking the silhouette, no shoulder blocks, and the tread-to-sidewall transition is a sharp crease rather than a rounded shoulder. (3) The sidewalls are blank. Real tyres carry raised brand lettering, a size code (205/55 R16 91V), DOT and E-mark codes, a rim protector rib and curved sidewall bulge. Here the sidewalls are flat discs, and that alone makes them look like rubber rings. (4) The bead and inner opening are a plain dark cylinder with no bead seat lip. (5) The material is uniformly mid-grey-black. Worn rubber goes slightly brown-grey and dusty on top surfaces, while tread grooves hold dirt. The brownish smears on the leaning tyre read as paint rather than dust. (6) The leaning tyre's contact with the ground and the stack is ambiguous in the side view, where it seems to touch only at a point and nearly floats.
suggestions: Raise radial segments to 48 (about 64 for the hero LOD) and use a 6-8 segment cross-section profile with a rounded shoulder, a sidewall bulge (max width about 1/3 up from the bead) and a 5 mm bead lip. About 1.5-2k tris per tyre. Instance one tyre mesh five times.

Bake a sidewall normal and AO map (one shared 1K) with raised lettering in a ring: brand, '205/55 R16 91V', DOT code, and a rim protector rib. Put an albedo-identical but rougher (0.9 vs 0.8) lettering mask on top.
Cut real tread grooves into the silhouette: 4 circumferential grooves 8 mm deep plus lateral sipes as normals only. Keep the groove floors darker and dustier.

Material: base albedo about 0.04-0.05 (very dark), roughness 0.85. Add a top-facing dust layer (albedo +0.06, slightly warm) driven by the world-up normal, and mud in the grooves near the ground. Remove the paint-like brown streaks.

Settle the leaning tyre physically: rest it on its tread at the bottom and against the stack edge at a single contact point, with a slight squash (about 1%) at the ground contact. Add a contact AO decal under the stack.
renderer_notes: Rubber with no specular environment looks plasticky grey in the shaded areas. A sky-reflection probe would help, but the faceting and blank sidewalls are asset issues.

summary: Correct A-frame pub-garden table construction with plank gaps and bolts; the wood surfaces are too uniform and the timber edges too crisp.
critique: The construction is right: an A-frame with splayed legs, bench bearers through-bolted to the legs, diagonal braces to a centre rail, top planks with gaps, two-plank benches, and visible bolt heads. Proportions match a 1.8 m table (top about 740, benches about 440). Issues: (1) All timber is perfectly square-edged. Pressure-treated softwood (planed all round) has about 5 mm rounded arrises, and the end grain is cut with slight checks and splits. (2) The wood texture is a wavy procedural grain with the same colour on every plank. Real weathered tables vary plank to plank (some greyer, some greener from treatment), have darker end grain, black weathering at joints and fasteners, lichen near the feet, and splits along the grain. The close-up grain looks like warped noise rather than flatsawn rings and knots. (3) No knots. (4) The legs end flat on the grass with no settling, mud or wear. (5) In the first view the top reads as a single slab because the plank gaps are too small or shadowed. (6) The bolts are just dots: no carriage bolt domes, washers or nuts on the far side. (7) There is no surface clutter or wear: rings, carved initials, a bird dropping, grey UV-bleached top surfaces versus browner protected undersides.
suggestions: Bevel all timber edges by 4-6 mm (2-segment bevel). It adds about 300 tris to the whole table and transforms the read under the sun.
Per-plank albedo variation (hue ±4%, value ±10%) and a random UV offset or rotation into a 2K wood atlas so no two planks share grain. Add 2-4 knots per plank as albedo plus normal.

Weathering: upward faces UV-greyed (desaturate 40%, lighten 10%), undersides and joints darker and browner, green algae on the lowest 100 mm of the legs, darker wet end grain. Drive it by world normal and height in the shader, at no texture cost.
Widen the top-plank gaps to 8-10 mm and give each plank a slight cup (2 mm) or random 0.5° twist so the top doesn't read as a slab.
Model carriage-bolt domes (16 mm, 6 tris) with square washers and nuts on the inner face of the leg-bearer joints. Add 2-3 end-grain checks as normal decals.
renderer_notes: Flat ambient makes the shadowed underside read lighter than it should. A contact shadow or AO under the table would ground it.

summary: Recognisable BMW-3-style saloon from the front, but the body is slab-sided and toy-like, the greenhouse construction has obvious errors, and the paint has no reflections.
critique: Nice touches: UK plates (white front, yellow rear) with a valid-looking registration, a kidney grille, LED DRL headlight strips, L-shaped tail-lights, a shark-fin antenna, mirrors, door handles, and multi-spoke alloys. But the car fails at the level of form: (1) The body side is a near-vertical slab with no shoulder line, no tumblehome, no wheel-arch flares or lips, and no sill line. Real cars have strong curvature from beltline to sill and a crisp character line. This one reads like an extruded profile. (2) The greenhouse is broken. The chrome window-surround frame stands proud of the body and sticks out past the C-pillar as a separate blade, the A-pillar frame overhangs the bonnet, and the rear screen sits as a flat recessed tray in the boot deck rather than flowing into the roof. From the rear three-quarter it looks like a roofless cabin with a window frame bolted on. (3) The proportions are off for a G20 (L 4709, H 1442, WB 2851). The bonnet is very long and flat and the front overhang reads long. The cabin looks set back and narrow relative to the body width (the greenhouse is inset too far, so the shoulders are too wide and flat on top). (4) The wheels are slightly small for the body. The tyres have thin sidewalls with no arch gap shading, and there are no dark wheel wells, so the wheels look stuck on. (5) The paint is a single flat blue with no clearcoat behaviour, no environment reflection and no panel-gap shading strong enough to read the doors. Panel lines are barely visible. (6) The underbody has no visible dark sill or rocker. (7) The bumpers have no separate lower diffuser or valance shapes.
suggestions: Fix the greenhouse first: make the side glass and the DLO trim a single loft that sits ON the body's beltline with 8-10° tumblehome, ending exactly at the C-pillar. Remove the protruding chrome blade. Make the rear screen a continuous surface from the roof trailing edge down to the boot lid at about 25-28° (no recess).

Rebuild the body section as a lofted profile with 6-8 cross-sections along the length: a convex side (about 30-40 mm of outward bow), a sharp shoulder character line about 80 mm below the beltline, a tucked-in sill, and flared wheel arches with a 15 mm lip. The body stays under 15-20k tris at LOD0.

Match G20 numbers: L 4.71, W 1.83, H 1.44, WB 2.85 m, front overhang about 0.82 m, rear about 1.04 m. Increase the wheel diameter to about 0.68 m (225/45 R18), the arch radius to wheel+35 mm, and add a black wheel-well liner inside each arch.

Car paint shader: clearcoat with a fresnel term and a sky-colour or IBL reflection (even a 64x64 cube or a 2-colour sky gradient). Base albedo blue about (0.03, 0.08, 0.25) linear, roughness 0.15 clearcoat over 0.4 base. Without reflections no car will look real.

Panel gaps: cut 3 mm dark grooves (geometry or normal plus AO decal) for the doors, bonnet, boot and fuel flap. Add a black plastic lower sill, a front splitter and rear diffuser shapes, and darken the glass with interior AO.
renderer_notes: The renderer has no SSR or environment reflection on paint and glass, which costs any car heavily. Please add at least a sky-colour reflection term to the shader for metallic and clearcoat materials. The body-shape and greenhouse problems are independent of that.

summary: A solid, believable 750 mm road cone with a rubber base, reflective sleeves and light scuffing; it needs moulding detail and better material response to go further.
critique: The shape, height and base footprint are right. The square base has rounded corners and a raised rim, two white retroreflective bands, a hollow tip opening, and believable dirt and scuff grime on the lower orange. It is one of the better small props. Remaining tells: (1) The cone body is a perfect smooth cone. Real UK cones have a slight change in taper near the top, a moulded lip at the tip, and the sleeve edges sit slightly proud (sleeves are separate film bands about 0.5 mm thick, with a visible edge and occasionally a peeling corner). (2) The reflective sleeves are flat light grey. Real Type 1 sleeves have a micro-prismatic sheen and a faint hex or cell pattern, and are bright under headlights but greyish in daylight. The grey value is plausible, but there is no texture at all. (3) The orange is a single uniform value. Real cones fade from UV, so the top is lighter and pinker and the lower part dirtier. There are some grime patches, but no road dust gradient. (4) The base is uniformly black rubber with no texture, no moulded lettering or recycled-rubber speckle, and no scuffing on the corners. (5) There is no ground contact shadow or squash, and the base edges look slightly floating.
suggestions: Add a 2 mm proud lip at each sleeve edge (2 extra rings) and a 4 mm rolled lip at the tip. Add a faint subtle taper change 100 mm below the tip. About +60 tris.
Sleeve material: albedo about 0.7, roughness 0.35, plus a fine hex micro-prism normal tile (shared 256 px). Add one per-instance random scuff or peeled corner mask.
Orange: vertical gradient, the top 10% lighter and more desaturated (UV fade), the bottom 15% dusty grey-brown. Add per-instance hue jitter ±3% so a row of cones doesn't look cloned.
Base: recycled-rubber speckle in the albedo (0.03-0.06), 'CHAPTER 8' or manufacturer lettering as a normal decal on one face, lighter worn corners (roughness up, albedo +0.05).
Add a small blob or contact-AO decal under the base to seat it on asphalt or grass.
renderer_notes: Retroreflection can't be shown without headlights or a view-aligned term. Consider a cheap view-dependent boost for sleeves at night.

summary: Reads as a John-Deere-like garden tractor with the right layout, but the bonnet is a blob, the tyres are wrong for turf, and the details are coarse.
critique: The layout is right: front engine bonnet with a grille, a steering column and wheel, a high-back seat over the rear wheels on a rear fender pan, a mid-mounted deck with front caster or anti-scalp wheels, footplates with tread pattern, a lift lever and throttle with red knobs, and 'AGRIMAX X43' decals in yellow. Problems: (1) The bonnet is a soft, inflated ovoid with no crisp feature lines. Real lawn tractors have a hood with sharp creases, headlight recesses, a separate grille surround, and a visible split line between the hood and the dash tower. The grille is a flat dark rectangle stuck on the nose. (2) The tyres have aggressive square knobbly treads like an ATV. Garden tractors use turf-saver tyres (shallow chevron or diamond blocks) to avoid damaging the lawn, which matters on a training ground. The front tyres look too wide and too large relative to the rears; on an X350, the fronts are 15x6 and the rears 20x10. (3) The seat is a thin single shell that floats on the fender with no visible pan, springs or adjust rail, and the backrest is a flat plate. (4) The deck is a flat black disc with no discharge chute, no belt cover, and no deck-height wheels at the right places. (5) The rear fender pan reads as a tray with a thick bulbous rim. The rear has no hitch plate or tail details beyond a couple of dark blocks. (6) The paint is uniform bright green with sparse white specks, which read as noise rather than chips. Real wear is mud on the lower panels and deck, grass clippings, scuffed footplates and faded paint on the hood top. (7) The dash and steering column are thin and simple: no gauges, key switch or fuel cap.
suggestions: Rebuild the hood as a lofted shape with a hard shoulder crease, a flat top, 2 inset headlight pockets with emissive lenses, and a separate grille frame with horizontal slats (normal map). Add a 3 mm split line to the dash tower. About 2-3k tris.

Swap to turf tyres: front 15x6-6, rear 20x10-8. Use a shallow diamond or chevron tread as a normal map on a smooth carcass with a rounded shoulder and yellow steel rims with 4-5 lug nuts and a valve. About 1k tris per wheel.
Seat: a moulded bucket with a 60 mm cushion, a rounded backrest top, a seat pan with a fore/aft slide rail and a visible pivot hinge to the fender. Add a hidden seat switch box underneath.

Deck: a domed top with a belt guard cover, a side discharge chute (or a mulch plug), 2 anti-scalp rollers at the front corners, and a height-adjust lever on the fender. Gauges, key and fuel cap as cheap decals plus small cylinders on the dash.
Wear: grass clipping and mud mask on the deck, tyres and lower body (world-height driven). UV-fade the hood top 10%. Real paint chips on edge highlights only (curvature mask), not random specks.
renderer_notes: Green-on-green against the lawn reduces contrast. That is a presentation issue, not an asset issue.

summary: Correct galvanised field gate type with the proper rail and brace pattern, but it is too thin and minimal: no hinge or latch hardware to speak of, and the posts are undersized and plain.
critique: This is the standard galvanised steel field gate: 5 horizontal rails, a centre stile, diagonal half-braces, a heavier top rail, hung on a timber hinge post and closing to a shorter timber shutting post with a small red latch detail. At distance it reads correctly. Close up: (1) All tubes look the same thin diameter. On a real gate the top rail is a larger oval or 48 mm tube, the stiles are about 42 mm and the intermediate rails are about 25-33 mm, and the rails are spaced closer at the bottom (stock-proofing). Here the spacing looks nearly even. (2) The hinge hardware is invisible. Field gates hang on large eye-and-hook hinges (a bolt-through hook on the post, an adjustable eye on the gate) top and bottom. They are the defining detail and are missing or tiny. (3) The latch is a small red blob. Real gates use a spring-loaded slide bolt or a Bristol latch with a catch plate on the shutting post. (4) The posts read as square, light-grey concrete rather than treated timber (oak or tanalised softwood, about 200x200 mm for the hanging post, with a weathered top cut at an angle). The shutting post is fine in height but the same plain material. (5) The galvanising is a uniform light silver, too clean and too metallic-reflective. Real galvanised steel is a matte mottled grey (spangle) with white-rust bloom and darker welds. (6) The welds and tube ends are not visible, and there are no end caps. (7) There is no ground interaction (no worn mud patch, rut or longer grass under the gate swing).
suggestions: Vary the tube diameters: top rail 50 mm oval (8-sided is fine), stiles 42 mm, rails 27 mm. Space the rails tighter at the bottom (about 150, 150, 200, 250, 300 mm from the ground up). Keep 6-sided tubes for the mid LOD. The total gate is still under 2k tris.

Model the hook-and-eye hinges: 2 hooks with 20 mm pins through the hanging post (bolt head and nut visible on the back) and 2 eye straps on the gate stile. Add a drop-bolt or Bristol latch on the closing stile and a catch plate on the shutting post. About 400 tris total.

Posts: a 200x200 mm hanging post and 150x150 mm shutting post in treated timber. Use a 1K tiling wood atlas with checks along the grain, a sloped weathered top cut, green-tinged base and a darker wet 200 mm band at the ground line.

Galvanised material: metallic 1.0, albedo about 0.55 grey with a large-scale spangle mottling (±8%), roughness 0.55-0.7, white-rust patches near welds and the bottom rail, and darker weld beads at each rail-stile joint.
Add a ground decal: a worn, muddy arc along the gate swing path and a tuft strip under the bottom rail, to seat it.
renderer_notes: Thin tubes shimmer and alias at distance. A pre-filtered thin-geometry LOD or alpha-tested impostor will help in-game. That is pipeline, not modelling.

summary: Convincing three-tier bowl with dense instanced seats, aisles, vomitories, crest lettering in the seats and LED ribbons between tiers; it lacks structural and surface detail at the close-up level.
critique: The scale reads like a real Premier League bowl: continuous tiers, consistent rake, radial aisles with yellow step nosings, handrails down the aisles, vomitory openings in the lower tier, fascia ribbons, and 'KIT FC' picked out in seat colour. Seats are individually modelled with backs, which is good. Weaknesses: (1) The vomitories are hard-edged grey boxes with flat interiors and no rails around the opening edge, no signage numbers and no shading inside, so they read as cutouts. (2) Tier fascias are flat dark bands. There are no balcony front details (glass or steel parapet, safety rail), no hospitality box glazing between tiers (a defining Premier League feature), and no camera gantry. (3) The seat colour is uniform. Real seats vary slightly from fading and replaced seats, have tip-up gaps, and show row letters and seat numbers. Under sun the seat red goes pink and washed out, and in shade near-black, with little in between. (4) The concrete risers are the same flat grey with no staining, drainage lines or expansion joints. (5) In the lower tier near the pitch, the front-row wall and the walkway are plain. (6) Upper-tier seating has corner gaps and joins that look abruptly cut at the corners (the corner sections in the overall view have odd wedge shapes). (7) Seats sit in very regular rows with no gangway steps' riser lighting.
suggestions: Add a hospitality and executive-box level between the lower and middle tiers: a continuous band of tinted glazing about 2.4 m tall with mullions every 3-4 m and interior emissive. It is cheap (one strip mesh plus a 1K atlas) and immediately says 'Premier League'.
Vomitories: add a 1.1 m steel balustrade around the 3 open edges, a lit soffit with a sign plate number decal, a darker AO gradient into the opening, and side walls with a 100 mm chamfer.

Seat material: per-instance albedo jitter (±5% value), a few faded or replaced seats (1-2%), and occasional tipped-up seats via a 2-pose instance. Cap the sun albedo for red seats at about 0.45 so they don't wash to pink.
Tier fronts: a glass or steel parapet with a top rail on each balcony edge, and a camera gantry plus press box on the main stand's upper tier.
Concrete: a tiled 1K concrete texture with streaking under each riser lip, drainage channels at aisle bottoms, and expansion joints every 6-8 m.
renderer_notes: Hard sun versus very dark shade (no GI bounce) makes seats in the shaded tiers almost black and the sunlit tier pink. Better ambient or bounce would help a lot here.

summary: A complete cantilevered ring roof with radial ribs and an underside truss, but the top surface is a flat, featureless white and the underside reads as plain grey planes.
critique: The roof forms a continuous rounded-rectangle ring, cantilevered to a clean inner edge with a dark fascia, supported by radial members visible from below and by the large concrete facade piers outside. The overall massing is plausible. But: (1) The top surface is a uniform matte white with thin radial lines and faint concentric bands. Real roofs show standing-seam metal sheeting or translucent polycarbonate panels near the inner edge, gutters, walkways, roof hatches, plant, lightning-protection runs and staining. It reads like a plastic tray. (2) The inner edge (leading edge) is a simple thick dark band. Leading edges carry the main compression truss, catwalk, PA speakers, floodlight rig and TV lighting. Here it is bare. (3) The underside is a flat grey soffit with small rib lines and evenly spaced tiny light dots. The secondary purlins and truss depth are too thin and too regular, and there is no visible depth of structure (real cantilevers are 3-6 m deep trusses at the root tapering to the tip). (4) The connection between the roof and the stand back (rear wall) shows no visible back-span or tie. (5) No translucent strip at the inner edge to bring light onto the pitch, which is standard in modern UK grounds.
suggestions: Top surface: a standing-seam metal normal map (300-400 mm seams running radially), roughness 0.45, light grey albedo about 0.65 with darker staining along seams and at the gutter. Add a 6-10 m translucent polycarbonate band at the inner edge (albedo 0.8, slight transmission or emissive in daylight).

Leading edge: model a triangular box truss about 3 m deep around the whole inner ring (instanced chord tubes plus diagonals, about 30 tris per bay), with a catwalk deck and floodlight fittings (see floodlights) attached.

Underside: deepen the radial cantilever trusses to about 4 m at the root tapering to 1 m at the tip. Use real diagonal lattice members (instanced) instead of thin lines. Add purlins every 2.5 m and gutter channels, with a darker soffit near the back wall (fake AO).
Add roof-top furniture: maintenance walkways with rails, 4-8 roof hatches, a few plant units at the corners and drainage outlets. All cheap instanced boxes.
renderer_notes: With no GI, the roof underside receives only flat ambient, so the structure loses all depth. Baked AO into the roof mesh vertex colours would help a great deal at no runtime cost.

summary: Strong massing with concrete piers rising through the roof edge and a diamond-pattern cladding skin, but the skin is monotonous and the ground level is underdeveloped.
critique: Massing works: a rounded-rectangle bowl, tall fluted concrete piers at regular intervals carrying the roof, a dark band at the roof line, a diamond-panel cladding skin, a club-colour sponsor sign, a ground-floor glazed band with entrances, a concourse plaza with trees, and lamps. Problems: (1) The cladding is a single flat diamond pattern over huge areas. Some panels on the upper left of one elevation have a random scattering of brighter, seemingly extruded diamonds. That reads as an artefact or z-fight rather than a design, and one curved corner elevation has a puffy 'cushion' pattern while the flat sides are smooth, which is inconsistent. (2) There is nothing at human scale between ground and roof: no stair cores, no glazed concourse levels, no turnstile blocks, no visible upper concourse or ramps, no signage beyond one banner. Real exteriors show concourse levels through the skin. (3) The ground level is a thin black band with a few small doors. Real stadia have turnstile banks with numbered gates, club shop frontage, ticket office, crowd barriers and bollards, and canopies over the entrances. (4) The piers are identical extruded profiles with 3 vertical grooves, and they read as concrete fins of constant section from ground to over the roof. There are no cap details or bearing connections where the roof meets them. (5) The plaza is a plain light-grey slab with a few trees and lamp posts: no paving pattern, kerbs, crowd-control barriers, bins or wayfinding. (6) The cladding panels have no thickness, reflections or gaps.
suggestions: Break the skin into 3 horizontal zones: a glazed ground level (4-5 m) with turnstile blocks and numbered gate signs, a mid band with concourse glazing visible through perforated or open panels, and the diamond cladding only on the upper 40%. Use one atlas with 3 rows and no extra draw calls.
Fix the random bright diamonds (likely an un-seeded per-panel offset or z-fighting). Either apply the cushion relief consistently on every elevation or remove it.

Add instanced ground-level furniture: turnstile kiosks (about 2x3 m) every 15-20 m with gate numbers, a club shop front with a sign, entrance canopies at the piers, crowd-control barriers and bollards. Add a paving pattern and kerbs to the plaza (1K tiling).
Piers: add a cap plate and a pin-joint bearing where the roof arm lands, a 50 mm chamfer and weather streaking down from the top (vertical streak mask).
Add stair or ramp cores at 2-4 corners, expressed as glazed or louvred towers, to break the long elevations.
renderer_notes: The long diagonal dark bands across the surrounding fields look like shadows from very tall off-frame objects or a texture seam. Please check whether they are intended. They are not part of the facade score.

summary: There are effectively no visible floodlights: the roof edge carries only tiny dots, with no luminaires, gantry or pylons.
critique: A roof-ring lit stadium is valid for a Premier League ground, but the lights must be visible as hardware. In these views: (1) The roof leading edge and underside show only small evenly spaced light-coloured dots or lines. There are no luminaire heads (about 0.6-0.8 m rectangular or round LED floods), no aiming angles, no catwalk or gantry, and no cable trays. (2) Nothing reads as a floodlight from the pitch, the stands or the aerial view. A player or broadcast camera would see 200-400 fittings ringing the roof edge. (3) No emissive or lens material is visible. The roof edge is the same grey as the rest.
suggestions: Add an instanced LED flood fitting (box housing 0.7x0.5x0.25 m, a dark finned rear heat sink, a light-grey front lens with a faint grid of LED dots as a normal or emissive map, and a yoke bracket). About 200 tris, 1 shared 512 px texture. Instance 250-350 along the leading-edge truss, in 2 staggered rows, each aimed at a pitch target point (orientation from a solver aiming at grid points on the pitch).
Mount them on a continuous catwalk gantry with handrails (instanced) along the inner roof edge, at 20-30 m above the pitch.
Give the lens an emissive term that fades in at dusk, plus a cheap view-facing glare sprite for night matches.
renderer_notes: No light-cone volumetrics are needed, but some sprite glow would sell night scenes.

summary: Correct markings, mowing stripes and a good-looking goal with hex netting; the turf lacks wear variation and the net hangs too rigidly.
critique: The pitch has alternating mown stripes, correct markings (halfway line, centre circle, boxes), corner flags, a technical-area dashed line, and goal frames that are the right size (7.32 x 2.44) with rounded white posts, a back frame and a hex mesh net. Shortfalls: (1) The turf is very uniform. Real elite pitches in match condition show subtle wear in the goalmouths and down the centre, a slightly different grass behind the goal lines, divots, and sharper edges where the paint sits on the grass (lines are slightly fuzzy, painted on the blades). The lines here are crisp and flat white. (2) In close views the turf texture reads as a coarse procedural noise, without visible blade direction from the mowing (stripes should shift with view direction due to blade lean, not be fixed colour bands). (3) The net is a rigid box: no sag along the roof and back, no tension towards the ground pegs, no bunching at the bottom, and the hex mesh is evenly flat. Real nets droop between supports. (4) The goal frame is plain white with no socket collar, net hooks or net clip detail, and the back support is a simple rectangle (the stanchions shape is fine). (5) The 3D 'carpet' advertising mat behind the goal looks like a flat white plane with a stretched logo. That is OK, but it has no thickness or bevel.
suggestions: Mowing stripes: make the stripe contrast view-dependent (lerp light/dark on dot(view, stripe direction)) so the stripes flip when viewed from the other end, as on TV. This is a shader-only change.

Add a wear mask: goalmouths, the centre circle and the linesman runs, with lighter, sparser, browner grass and a few divots as decals. Paint lines with soft 15-20 mm edges and a slight green bleed through.

Nets: deform the net mesh with a simple catenary sag (60-120 mm between supports on the roof and back) and a 150 mm bunch at the bottom pegged to the ground. Use instanced pegs or ground hooks. Cheap to bake once per goal.
Goal frame: add net-hook clips every 400 mm, ground socket collars and a slightly rounded elliptical profile for the posts (120x100 mm typical at elite level).
3D carpet: give it 15 mm thickness with a bevelled edge and a slight curl, so it doesn't read as a decal.
renderer_notes: The shaded half of the pitch goes very dark green (no sky bounce), and the line contrast drops. A stronger sky ambient on grass would fix most of it.

summary: Proper perspex-shell team shelters with padded seats and a telescopic tunnel in club red, though the tunnel mouth is a plain box and the details are coarse.
critique: Positioned correctly either side of the halfway line, with a telescopic tunnel extension, curved polycarbonate canopies, rows of bucket seats in dark grey and a red plinth. That is all correct for a Premier League technical area. Problems: (1) The tunnel extension is a smooth red half-barrel with white edge hoops but no fabric or ribbed segment structure. Real tunnels are concertina sections with visible overlapping hoops, a club crest on the side, and a vinyl skirt at the ground. (2) The tunnel portal in the stand is a plain grey concrete box with a grey door at the back. Elite grounds dress the portal with club branding, a 'This is ...' sign, lit soffit and glazed doors. (3) The dugout shells are clear arches with thin white frame lines, but the polycarbonate has no visible tint, edge thickness or reflections, so they read as wireframes. (4) The seats are dark grey uniform blocks without headrests, stitching or club logos. Premier League dugouts use padded racing-style seats with logos. (5) There is no technical-area detail: no fourth official's board or desk, no water bottle crates, no cable covers.
suggestions: Tunnel extension: 4-5 telescoping segments, each 0.1 m larger than the last, with overlapping rim hoops and a crest decal on each side. About 1k tris. Add a black rubber skirt at the base.
Tunnel portal: a branded surround (club colour band and sign plate), an emissive soffit light strip, and glazed double doors with push bars at the back. Add a darker AO gradient inside.
Dugout canopy: a polycarbonate material with 6-8 mm visible edge thickness, a light blue-grey tint (transmission 0.85), a fresnel reflection, and a club decal on the back panel.

Seats: a padded bucket with a headrest and an embroidered crest decal (shared 512 px). Instance 12-14 per dugout. Add a fourth-official desk and an electronic substitution board prop between the dugouts.
renderer_notes: Transparent polycarbonate without reflections or refraction is hard to sell in a forward renderer. Even a simple fresnel-weighted sky reflection would help.

summary: Convincing LED perimeter boards and two-tier ribbon boards with legible fictional brands, plus corner scoreboards with a live score; they need LED pixel character and support hardware.
critique: This is the strongest stadium part. Perimeter boards carry a varied set of fictional sponsors with consistent typography (a tagline small, a logo and a wordmark), continuous ribbon boards ring two tier fascias, and two corner big screens show a 'KIT FC 2-1 ROVERS' scoreboard with match time and a sponsor. Remaining issues: (1) The boards read as printed vinyl, not LED. Real LED perimeter boards glow (emissive, slightly overexposed whites), show a fine pixel grid close up, and have a dark bezel between modules every 1-1.92 m. Here the colours are matte and module seams are absent. (2) The perimeter boards have no visible thickness, rear frame, angled support legs or base. At the pitch-level close-up the board is a clean flat slab with no back structure or cable. (3) Ribbon boards are an identical repeating sequence all round the bowl, so the repetition is obvious in wide shots. (4) The big screens are flat panels with a thin border. Real screens have a deep housing with a rear access walkway and support structure hung from the roof truss. (5) The perimeter board run along the goal line ends abruptly, and some boards at the corners overlap.
suggestions: LED look: an emissive term (1.5-2x albedo in daylight) plus a fine pixel-grid normal and albedo modulation (10 mm pitch, 256 px tile) that fades in only near the camera. Add a 15 mm dark module seam every 1.0 m along the run.

Perimeter boards: model a 0.9-1.0 m tall cabinet that is 0.25 m deep with a black rear, angled A-frame support legs every 2 m, and a rubber kick-strip foam pad on top. About 60 tris per module, instanced.
Randomise the ribbon-board sponsor order per tier and per side, and run 1-2 tiers as an animated scroll offset in the shader for life.
Big screens: a 1-1.5 m deep housing box with louvred sides, a rear catwalk and 2-4 hanger struts to the roof truss. Add a slight emissive bloom on the screen.
Check the corner board joins: mitre or leave a 0.3 m gap with a padded end cap instead of overlapping.
renderer_notes: Without bloom or tonemapped emissive, LED boards will always look printed. A cheap emissive plus bloom pass would raise this part noticeably.
